newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya still hit by IMF decision,neighbours benefit.
newsitem.headline: Kenya still hit by IMF decision,neighbours benefit.

text.p: The IMF's halting of a key aid package has jolted Kenya's thriving markets but has turned into a mixed blessing for the national currencies in neighbouring Tanzania and Uganda.
Currency and equity markets in Kenya, East Africa's economic powerhouse, are still struggling following the July 31 decision to freeze the IMF's $205 million aid package, citing corruption.
The besieged Kenyan shilling swifly buckled under pressure from foreign investors pulling out and on Tuesday sank to a record official low to the dollar of 70.48, 18.45 percent down since July 31.
Foreign currency dealers estimate that just over $100 million has left the country since the IMF move of which 10 percent was pulled out by local investors seeking a safer place to put their money.
Some of this went to Tanzania, where the Tanzanian shilling has posted daily gains -- though marginal in the past week -- because of surplus of dollars for sale, financial experts said.
But in Uganda, the Ugandan shilling has dropped to its lowest against the dollar this year because of a surge in dollar demand, partly from investors buying dollars to sell in Kenya.
Since the IMF decision on Kenya, the Tanzanian shilling has strengthened 0.813 percent against the dollar while the Ugandan shilling has weakened by a total of 1.6 percent, dealers said.
A Tanzanian dealer said between $3 million and $4 million was trading daily on the the interbank market, an estimated increase of up to $12 million per month from the same period six months ago.
Banking sources said unconfirmed estimates of inflows of hard currency from Kenya were up to $12 million per week. But much of this was believed arriving by non-official channels.
"What I can say is several people have shown interest in doing business in Tanzania while the Kenyan currency is losing value. We have had inquiries from Nairobi," said a dealer.
The Tanzanian shilling was posted at a commercial mean of 619.7301 to the dollar from 619.8687 on Monday, a 0.02 percent gain. The Ugandan shilling on Tuesday was unchanged at 1092.5 to the dollar.

At the heart of the shilling's bruising two weeks is a multi-million dollar scandal involving a Kenyan company Goldenberg International, civil servants and businessmen accused by the opposition of being protected because of political links.
The shilling's crisis since the IMF decision worsed on Tuesday after news from the World Bank that it was contemplating withholding further aid to Kenya until Kenya tackled graft.
"This is a vote of no confidence," one senior dealer said.
A World Bank official said on Monday the World Bank delayed paying part of a loan to Kenya and would find it hard to hand over money until the government addressed corruption concerns.
The official, who asked not to be named, said in Washington that the bank shared the concerns of the IMF about corruption.

"The second tranche of our structural adjustment loan had been suspended because policy conditions (on privatisation) had not been met, but we would find it difficult to release this money until the IMF programme is back on track," he said.
He said Kenya received one tranche of the loan last year, but the second tranche of just over $71 million was not paid.
An energy sector loan, approved by the World Bank board in Washington in June, could also be in doubt because the IMF had singled out energy as a sector suspected of mismanagement.

The official said World Bank credits for social and environmental programmes were still being paid, although government cash shortages due to the IMF decision to halt its $205 million loan package meant loans for development projects could lapse if the government could no longer fund its share. ($1=70.48 Kenyan shillings)
